name: Neem twig / miswak

card.summary: Traditional chewing sticks with a long history; small observational studies on gum health, no whitening trials.
card.note: Evidence is observational; no whitening trials.

quick.overview:
Miswak and neem twigs are chewing sticks used as natural toothbrushes, especially in the Middle East and South Asia.

Small observational studies link miswak use to better gum health; no trials of whitening were found.
quick.mechanism: The frayed fibers clean mechanically, and plant compounds are believed to have antibacterial activity.
quick.risks: Twig chewing has no specific harms in the sources reviewed; neem oil is toxic to small children.

lead: Chewing sticks are twigs whose frayed ends serve as natural toothbrushes, used to clean teeth and freshen the breath. The best known is miswak, from the Salvadora persica (arak) tree, traditionally used across the Middle East and Africa; neem (Azadirachta indica) twigs, called datun in South Asia, are used the same way.[1][2][3] People who use them aim for cleaner, brighter-looking teeth, healthier gums and fresher breath, all of which feed into the look of a smile.[1][4]

The outer bark is peeled away to expose fibres that act as bristles, and the tip can be trimmed to renew the surface.[1] Practitioners cite tradition, antibacterial plant compounds and mechanical plaque removal as the reasons for use; hadith are reported to recommend its use, and fibrous chewing sticks have been used since antiquity.[1]

The research base includes randomized trials and systematic reviews. A 2022 meta-analysis of randomized trials found miswak used alone was comparable to a toothbrush for plaque and gingivitis, and better than a toothbrush alone when used as an adjunct.[5] Reviews also describe whitening properties among reported effects, although whitening is not the main outcome measured in the trials.[4]

chain: Fibrous twig mechanically cleans teeth and releases plant compounds
Less plaque and gum inflammation, fresher breath
angle.text: Users chew or brush with a peeled miswak or neem twig as a low-cost alternative or addition to a toothbrush, aiming for cleaner-looking teeth and fresher breath. Trial data focus on plaque and gum health, which underlie how a smile looks.

infobox: Salvadorine, benzylisothiocyanate, fluoride, calcium, salicylic acid

paras: The user strips the outer bark to expose the inner fibres, which work as bristles, and the end can be trimmed and re-peeled for a fresh brushing surface.[1] In the Maghreb, "miswak" can also refer to a different walnut-wood tool.[1]

Wikipedia lists traditional beliefs among users that the stick strengthens gums, prevents decay, eases toothache, freshens breath and sharpens taste, and flags many of these as uncited.[1] Religious guidance recommends use at various times, such as before ablution and prayer.[1]

Salvadorine and benzylisothiocyanate are believed to be responsible for miswak's antibacterial activity, and it contains insoluble fluoride, calcium and salicylic acid.[1] A 2010 Pharmacognosy Reviews article profiles the plant Salvadora persica.[6] Neem has a long history in Indian traditional medicine, and the neem article states that clinical evidence for medicinal benefits is insufficient.[2]

The 2022 Journal of Ethnopharmacology meta-analysis pooled randomized trials of miswak (Salvadora persica and Azadirachta indica). Used alone, miswak was comparable to a toothbrush for plaque and gingivitis, with no statistically significant difference; as an adjunct to a toothbrush it was significantly better for plaque and gingivitis. The authors noted that included trials reported poorly on technique and frequency and called for more clinical studies.[5]

A 2019 meta-analysis in BMC Oral Health pooled 18 trials of Salvadora persica mouthrinses and found significantly lower plaque scores and cariogenic bacterial counts than placebo, but a smaller reduction than chlorhexidine. The authors suggested the rinse could serve as an alternative for long-term use.[7]

A 2020 evidence-based review in the Saudi Journal of Biological Sciences summarised studies of miswak in ten forms including chewing stick, toothpaste and mouthwash, and reported positive findings for plaque, gingivitis, cariogenic activity, gingival wound healing, whitening properties and biocompatibility.[4] Older observational data include a study of 203 people in Sudan with better periodontal status in miswak users than toothbrush users and a study of 480 Saudi adults linking frequent use to lower need for periodontal treatment; a 2005 laboratory comparison found miswak extract less antimicrobial than chlorhexidine or cetylpyridinium chloride.[1]

Neem oil is described as toxic to small children, and neem may be associated with miscarriage, infertility and low blood sugar; these concern ingestion of products rather than chewing twigs.[2] A 2023 letter in the British Dental Journal titled "Miswak misuse" comments on improper use of the stick.[8]

Randomized and controlled trials include a 2007 trial in Caries Research in which rinsing with miswak extract produced a prolonged rise in plaque pH compared with water,[9] a 2017 randomized trial of a miswak-extract toothpaste on gingival inflammation,[10] a 2017 trial comparing fluoridated miswak with toothbrushing and fluoride toothpaste on plaque removal and fluoride release,[11] a 2018 clinical trial of the chemical effects of Salvadora persica chewing sticks on plaque, subgingival microbiota and gingival inflammation,[12] and a 2021 blinded randomized trial comparing 40 percent miswak mouthwash with 0.12 percent chlorhexidine for gingivitis.[13] Systematic reviews summarise these trials.[4][5][7] The outcomes measured are plaque, gingivitis and bacterial counts; no trial found measured tooth colour change as its main outcome.

timeline.event: The World Health Organization recommends chewing sticks for oral hygiene.[1]
An international consensus report on oral hygiene concludes more research is needed.[1]
A laboratory comparison finds miswak extract less antibacterial than chlorhexidine.[1]
A meta-analysis of randomized trials compares miswak with toothbrushing for plaque and gingivitis.[5]
